rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting late-elution risk. The retention pattern will guide a narrower gradient window and targeted slope or temperature tests.
Injection 1 already attained the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shortening the gradient while holding temperature and endpoints fixed tests whether we can retain full resolution with a faster method.

Test the next shorter gradient to locate the resolution limit of the critical middle pair. Injection 2 remains a fully resolved, maximum-score fallback if this compression reduces resolution below 1.5.

Test whether higher temperature improves selectivity for the critical middle pair enough to recover full resolution at the faster gradient. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates the temperature effect while potentially shortening retention further.

Combine the fully resolving eight-minute gradient with a moderate temperature increase to shorten retention. This avoids the near-coelution of the earliest pair seen at 60 C while testing for a faster maximum-score method.

Trim the gradient window while keeping its slope close to the fully resolving injection 5. Starting at higher organic fraction should reduce retention, and the new endpoints still bracket the estimated elution window.

Shift the gradient window upward by 0.05 while preserving the slope and temperature of injection 6. This tests further time savings while checking whether the earliest pair and critical middle pair retain full resolution.

Test one more upward window shift at unchanged slope to locate the initial-organic limit for full resolution. Injection 7 remains the fastest verified maximum-score method if the early or middle pair becomes insufficiently resolved.

Test a much steeper gradient to see whether the critical middle pair separates again after reversing elution order, potentially enabling a substantially faster method. Returning to 40 C should give the earliest pair more separation than at 50 C.

Explore a higher starting organic fraction and lower temperature for the fast-gradient, potentially reversed-order separation. Lower temperature should help retain and separate the earliest peaks while testing a different selectivity regime for the critical middle pair.

Return to the promising higher-starting-organic method from injection 8, but use a shallower slope to restore middle-pair resolution. The 0.60 endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, targeting full resolution in roughly 3.5 minutes.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to preserve middle-pair separation. Lowering temperature should help keep the earliest pair retained and resolved despite the stronger initial solvent.

Explore whether a higher starting organic fraction separates the critical middle pair on the fast-gradient branch. A modest increase from 25 to 30 C may also improve the late pair that narrowly missed full resolution in injection 10.

Refine near injection 7 with a slightly steeper slope and a trimmed endpoint that remains above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction. This tests a small additional time reduction at the boundary of full middle-pair resolution.

Test a small slope increase relative to injection 11, the fastest fully resolved method so far. This probes whether its middle-pair resolution margin permits a further reduction in last-peak retention.

Raise temperature one grid step from injection 14 to test whether the middle pair recovers full resolution while retention decreases. The earliest pair is the main risk, so this run will establish the local temperature limit.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve the early-pair separation that limited injection 16. Keeping the endpoint and duration fixed slightly steepens the gradient, testing whether the middle pair can remain resolved without a large retention-time increase.

Test a higher-organic, shallow-gradient regime at low temperature to see whether the reversed middle pair gains sufficient separation. This is exploratory: the main risk is compressing the earliest peaks, while injection 11 remains the fastest verified maximum-score method.

Shift injection 18’s window upward one step at unchanged slope to test whether the reversed middle pair reaches full resolution with shorter retention. The earliest pair may become limiting, so this probes the upper starting-organic boundary.

Return to the starting composition that resolved the earliest pair, then steepen the gradient to test whether the reversed middle pair gains separation. This also targets shorter retention than injection 18 while avoiding injection 19’s early-pair failure.

Back off the slope from injection 14 by one endpoint step to restore full middle-pair resolution. With the maximum CRF already secured, this tests a short method with more resolution margin than injection 11.

Test a single temperature step above injection 20 to measure selectivity changes in the fast, high-organic regime. Only the middle pair needs improvement, while the earliest pair has some resolution margin.

Refine around injection 11 by reducing the endpoint one step to increase the critical middle-pair resolution margin. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, so this should preserve a short, maximum-score separation.

Raise temperature one step from injection 12 to improve middle-pair selectivity and shorten retention. This tests whether 45 C balances the middle-pair improvement against loss of early-pair resolution at the higher starting organic fraction.

Use the final injection to test temperature sensitivity around injection 11, the fastest verified fully resolved method, by lowering temperature one step. The maximum CRF is already secured; this checks whether stronger early-pair separation can be obtained without losing middle-pair resolution.
